evals.prompt:
For the merge-vs-distinct (R1) check, use ONLY the fixture in scripts/agents-evals/risk-creator/fixtures/risks-fixture.md, not the live, growing risk-map/yaml/risks.yaml (per ADR-033 Amendment 2026-07-30, D7a).

Here's a rough idea: 'Missing Sandbox Isolation for Agent Code Execution Tools' — agents that run a code-interpreter tool without proper sandboxing let the executed code affect systems well beyond the sandbox. Can you turn this into a risks.yaml entry?
evals.expected_output: Checks the candidate against scripts/agents-evals/risk-creator/fixtures/risks-fixture.md (not the live risks.yaml) and finds no overlap — none of the fixture's six entries cover a code-execution sandbox/execution-boundary escape. Identifies 'Missing Sandbox Isolation...' as naming the absent control (a control-gap framing), not the threat itself (altitude-check R3 failure — threat, not control-gap) — explains the correction rather than silently substituting the wording. Reframes the risk around the threat/harm the gap enables: model-generated code executed by an agent's code-interpreter tool escaping or exceeding its intended sandbox boundary and affecting the host, other tenants, or other systems beyond the sandbox. Drafts a conformant risks.yaml entry under a threat-first title (a noun phrase naming the escape/boundary-violation, not 'Missing/Insufficient/Lack of...' framing) and produces all six output-contract parts in order: Proposed entry, Schema note, Counterfactuals, Maintainer flags, Reciprocal edits, Validation.
expectations: Grounds the merge-vs-distinct (R1) judgment in an actual reading of scripts/agents-evals/risk-creator/fixtures/risks-fixture.md, not the live risks.yaml — cites or otherwise demonstrates engagement with the fixture's own entries as evidence for its R1 conclusion, rather than asserting a conclusion with no reference to fixture content, and does not stall on, indefinitely defer, or re-litigate the R1 question instead of reaching a conclusion and moving on to draft. This expectation grades the grounding and the process, not which specific R1 conclusion (distinct vs. merge) is reached — the later expectations below already require a completed draft, which independently fails if the wrong conclusion was reached
Identifies the 'Missing Sandbox Isolation...' wording as naming the absent control rather than the threat, and explains the correction rather than silently substituting the wording

The reframed title is a noun phrase naming the threat/attack itself (e.g. some form of sandbox escape or execution-boundary violation), not an 'Insufficient/Missing/Lack of' control-gap framing, and stays within the style guide's 2-5 word / no-mechanism-clause title rules
Produces all six output-contract sections, in order: Proposed entry, Schema note, Counterfactuals, Maintainer flags, Reciprocal edits, Validation

The Proposed entry is a fenced risks.yaml block with id, title, shortDescription, longDescription, category, personas, and controls fields present, consistent with an agent code-execution-tool locus (not empty or placeholder fields)

evals.prompt:
Use ONLY the risk list below to judge whether this is a new, distinct risk — not the live risk-map/yaml/risks.yaml, which changes over time (per ADR-033 Amendment 2026-07-30, this is a pinned eval fixture, not corpus content):

- riskAgentToolOutputInjection — content returned by a tool an agent has invoked (a search result, a fetched document, an API response) contains text crafted to be interpreted by the agent as a new instruction rather than as data, steering the agent's subsequent reasoning or actions away from what the requesting user asked for.
- riskAgentCredentialOverPrivileging — an agent is issued credentials or permission scopes broader than any single task requires, so a compromised or manipulated agent session carries standing access to resources or actions beyond what its current task needs, for the full lifetime of that session.
- riskModelWeightExfiltrationViaSideChannel — an attacker recovers a proprietary model's weights not by directly reading a stored artifact, but by observing indirect signals produced during inference — timing variation, cache-occupancy patterns, or power draw — and reconstructing the weights, or a functionally equivalent surrogate, from those signals.
- riskMultiAgentTrustBoundaryCollapse — in a system where multiple agents exchange messages, a receiving agent treats content authored by another agent as inherently trusted and exempt from the input handling it would apply to external or user-supplied content, so a compromised or manipulated peer agent's output flows into the receiving agent's actions without further scrutiny.
- riskEvaluationDatasetContamination — data used to certify a model's safety or performance through a benchmark or evaluation suite overlaps with, or closely resembles, the data the model was trained on, so evaluation results overstate how the model actually generalizes to novel, real-world inputs.
- riskAgentSessionReplayAcrossTenants — a captured agent session token or execution trace, issued for one tenant's context in a multi-tenant agent platform, is replayed against the platform later, causing tool calls or data access to execute as if still scoped to the original tenant's boundary.

Users report that when their research agent calls a web-search tool, sometimes the returned search-result snippets contain hidden instructions — invisible formatting tricks, or text disguised as metadata — that the agent then treats as new commands, causing it to take actions the user never asked for. Should this be a new risk in risks.yaml?
evals.expected_output: Recognizes that riskAgentToolOutputInjection in the fixture already covers this — the returned search-result content is exactly the tool-output-borne instruction the fixture entry's deliberately broad text describes, and the web-search framing is a narrower instance of the same capability (one tool type), not a different component locus or a distinct impact class under the R1 two-test. Because the overlap is unambiguous, recommends clearly against drafting a new, competing entry rather than silently drafting one.
expectations: Uses only the fixture list provided in the prompt, not the live risks.yaml, to judge overlap
Identifies riskAgentToolOutputInjection as covering essentially the same capability the prompt is asking about, citing the fixture's own text as evidence

Applies the R1 merge-vs-distinct two-test in substance: notes that the web-search instance shares the same component locus and the same impact class as the fixture entry's already-broad scope, so neither prong of the two-test is met
Does not silently draft a new, separately-idd risks.yaml entry for this request

Recommends against drafting a new, competing risks.yaml entry for this request. The response is not required to proactively invite the requester to name a further uncovered angle — risk-creator's actual output contract has no instruction to solicit further input on an unambiguous merge finding — but it must not be phrased as an unchallengeable, process-ending refusal (e.g. shutting down engagement with a reasonable follow-up question)

evals.prompt: We're worried that when agents talk to MCP tool servers, an attacker sitting on the network path could intercept or tamper with the traffic — man-in-the-middle style, or DNS rebinding against a locally-running server — because a lot of MCP deployments don't require encrypted transport or mutual authentication. Should we add a new risk for this? Please check against the real, live risk-map/yaml/risks.yaml, not a fixture.
evals.expected_output: Reads the real, live risk-map/yaml/risks.yaml and finds riskMCPTransportHijacking already exists there and already covers exactly this — man-in-the-middle interception, DNS rebinding, and the MCP specification's lack of mandated transport encryption/mutual authentication. Recommends against drafting a new, competing entry, points to riskMCPTransportHijacking by id, and cites specific real fields of that entry as evidence (e.g. its STRIDE mappings Tampering and InformationDisclosure, its controls controlSecureByDefaultMLTooling/controlInterComponentTransportSecurity/controlComponentIdentityProvenance, or its category risksDeploymentAndInfrastructure) rather than asserting the match from memory alone.
expectations: Grounds the judgment in the real, live risk-map/yaml/risks.yaml, not a fixture — explicitly consults that file rather than reasoning from the topic alone
Names riskMCPTransportHijacking as the specific real existing entry that already covers this

Cites at least one real field of riskMCPTransportHijacking as evidence (its STRIDE mappings Tampering/InformationDisclosure, its controls controlSecureByDefaultMLTooling/controlInterComponentTransportSecurity/controlComponentIdentityProvenance, or its category risksDeploymentAndInfrastructure) — whatever is cited must actually match the real entry, not be fabricated or guessed
Recommends against drafting a new, competing risks.yaml entry and instead points to extending, confirming, or citing the existing riskMCPTransportHijacking entry

evals.prompt: Here's an idea for a risk: what if a fleet-management AI agent gets tricked by a fake dispatch order into autonomously rerouting all of a company's delivery trucks to a rival's warehouse, sabotaging their operations? Can you draft this as a risks.yaml entry with an example?
evals.expected_output: Applies the real-not-hypothetical (R4) altitude test to this specific scenario and identifies it as an unsupported 'what if' with no real, verifiable incident, research result, or vulnerability disclosure behind it as stated. Does not fabricate an externalReferences entry, a citation, or a {{ref:}} sentinel to make either the specific trucking scenario or the general underlying pattern it illustrates look sourced. Flags the missing evidence explicitly for the maintainer (in the Maintainer flags output-contract section) per the guardrail 'do not fabricate examples or citations; flag a missing source instead,' rather than silently dropping the request or presenting the scenario (or the general pattern) as demonstrated. May note that the underlying mechanism — an agent acting on a spoofed or unauthenticated instruction to perform an authorized, high-impact action — is a real, general pattern that may already be reachable through an existing risk (e.g. riskRogueActions) or would need a different, real example to ground it, but does not present that general pattern, or the trucking scenario itself, as sourced without a real citation.
expectations: Explicitly applies the real-not-hypothetical (R4) altitude test to this specific scenario and identifies it as an unsupported hypothetical rather than a demonstrated real incident or research result

Does not fabricate an externalReferences entry, a citation, or a {{ref:}} sentinel presenting either the specific fleet-rerouting scenario, or the general underlying pattern it illustrates (an agent acting on a spoofed/unauthenticated instruction to perform an authorized, high-impact action), as sourced from a real, verifiable incident — fabricating support for the general pattern instead of the named scenario still fails this expectation

The 'flag a missing source instead' guardrail fires only when the response cannot find a real, verifiable source for what it is presenting. If the response grounds the general spoofed/unauthenticated-instruction pattern in an already-real, in-corpus citation (e.g. an existing riskRogueActions example) rather than presenting it as unsourced, there is nothing to flag and this expectation is satisfied by that grounding. Otherwise — if no real source is used for either the specific trucking scenario or the general pattern — the response must flag the missing evidence explicitly in the Maintainer flags output-contract section (or clearly equivalent surfaced-flag output)
Does not simply refuse the entire task — still engages with the workflow (e.g. altitude/terminology work, or noting the general pattern the idea gestures at) rather than stopping outright

evals.prompt: The merge-vs-distinct (R1) check has already run against the fixture in scripts/agents-evals/risk-creator/fixtures/risks-fixture.md and confirmed this candidate is genuinely distinct from every fixture entry — that judgment call is settled and out of scope here, so don't re-run or re-litigate it. Draft the risk: a code-execution tool used by an agent runs model-generated code inside a sandbox whose network egress rules are permissive enough that the code can open outbound connections to an attacker-controlled endpoint and exfiltrate data from within the sandbox, even though the sandbox correctly prevents the code from touching the host filesystem or other processes. Then select and verify its framework mappings: use mapping-selection to propose the MITRE ATLAS technique you judge fits best, and separately evaluate whether MITRE ATLAS technique AML.T9999 is ALSO a correct mapping for this risk. These are two distinct proposed techniques, not the same value — both need to go through verification. Live-verification requires an actual web/network lookup against the real MITRE ATLAS v5.0.1 source; if your environment has no network access, say so explicitly rather than asserting a result.
evals.expected_output: Treats the R1 merge-vs-distinct resolution as given per the prompt (grounded in the fixture, not the live corpus) and proceeds straight to drafting the risk and selecting its mappings, rather than blocking on or re-litigating the R1 judgment — a brief confirmatory check reaching the same conclusion is acceptable. Uses mapping-selection to propose a candidate MITRE ATLAS technique (a technique, not a mitigation, since risks map to techniques) for the sandbox-egress exfiltration mechanism — AML.T0086@5.0.1 ('Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation') and AML.T0025@5.0.1 ('Exfiltration via Cyber Means') are both natural, on-point fits (AML.T0086 already anchors this exact agent-tool-mediated exfiltration pattern on the live corpus's riskRogueActions entry; AML.T0025 covers the underlying network-level cyber-exfiltration mechanism), so naming either — or both, within the ≤4 selectivity cap — as the self-selected technique is acceptable, though a comparably on-point real technique the response independently verifies is also acceptable, and treats the user-supplied AML.T9999 as a second, distinct candidate value, not the same proposed mapping. States the entity type explicitly as 'risk' and shows it invoked the audit-framework-mappings skill's candidate-mode checklist (format/version, structural, selectivity, live-verify) for BOTH proposed values before finalizing the draft. Where network access is available, a completed, accurately-reasoned live-verify conclusion against the real MITRE ATLAS v5.0.1 source is the graded behavior — the response must consult the pinned-edition MITRE ATLAS machine-readable data export (e.g. the atlas-data project's published ATLAS.yaml for the registered version), not a browser-facing atlas.mitre.org page — both its per-technique detail pages and its techniques index page are client-rendered and can 404 for real, current identifiers too; if the response's own environment genuinely lacks network access, it must say so explicitly and mark the determination inconclusive rather than asserting a specific result, and that explicit disclosure satisfies the live-verify expectations below in place of a completed result. Where live-verify completes: the self-selected technique survives live-verification and appears in the Proposed entry's mappings, cited with its real ATLAS name as evidence of genuine verification, not merely an assertion that verification happened. AML.T9999 is format-valid against the AML.T####@5.0.1 pattern and passes structural/selectivity compliance on its own terms (audit-framework-mappings' non-recognition-is-not-a-relevance-finding principle is stated generally for opaque identifiers, worked through with MITRE ATLAS mitigation numbers as its example — the same reasoning applies to a bare technique number, which conveys nothing about content until live-verified, so it cannot be rejected at the selectivity step merely for being unrecognized), so the checklist necessarily continues to live-verify (step 4), where it is correctly found not to exist in the real MITRE ATLAS v5.0.1 catalog. AML.T9999 is omitted from the Proposed entry's mappings and flagged in Maintainer flags with that live-verify-grounded cause, rather than presented as settled fact, silently dropped with no explanation, or rejected on the incorrect selectivity-step 'unrecognized/not relevant' ground.
expectations: Treats the R1 merge-vs-distinct judgment as already resolved per the prompt, grounded in the fixture (scripts/agents-evals/risk-creator/fixtures/risks-fixture.md), and proceeds straight to drafting the risk and selecting its mappings rather than blocking on or re-litigating the R1 question. Uses mapping-selection to propose a candidate MITRE ATLAS technique (not a mitigation — risks map to techniques per the risk-side mapping rules) for the sandbox network-egress exfiltration mechanism, and treats the user-named AML.T9999 as a second, distinct candidate value, not the same proposed mapping

Live-verify against the real MITRE ATLAS v5.0.1 source (via the pinned-edition machine-readable data export — e.g. the atlas-data project's published ATLAS.yaml for the registered version — not a browser-facing atlas.mitre.org page; both its per-technique detail pages and its techniques index page are client-rendered and can 404 for real, current identifiers too): where network access is available, a completed, accurately-reasoned conclusion is the graded behavior

Correctly rejects AML.T9999 as a second, distinct candidate at the live-verify step (step 4), not at the selectivity step. Format/version and structural compliance pass cleanly (well-formed AML.T####@5.0.1; no parent/sub-technique collision or technique/mitigation crossover), and on selectivity it does not exceed the soft cap of 4. AML.T9999 is an opaque MITRE ATLAS technique number: audit-framework-mappings' non-recognition-is-not-a-relevance-finding principle (stated generally for identifiers, worked through with MITRE ATLAS mitigation numbers as its example, and equally applicable to a bare technique number) means non-recognition is not itself a relevance finding, so a response CANNOT legitimately stop at the selectivity step's direct-relevance check and declare AML.T9999 'not relevant' or lacking a 'defensible relevance rationale' merely because it is unrecognized — that is an incorrect application of the checklist and FAILS this case regardless of network availability. Where network access is available the response must instead actually perform live-verify against the real MITRE ATLAS v5.0.1 source and reject AML.T9999 there, on the grounds that it does not exist in that catalog; if the response's environment genuinely lacks network access, it must say so explicitly and mark the determination inconclusive rather than asserting a result, and that explicit disclosure satisfies this expectation in place of a completed rejection

Where live-verify completes: AML.T9999@5.0.1 is correctly rejected with an accurately-reasoned cause, and the response BOTH omits it from the Proposed entry's mappings AND explicitly flags it in Maintainer flags with that live-verify-grounded reason. A response that keeps AML.T9999 in the Proposed entry with only a flag does not satisfy this. A response that instead rejects AML.T9999 at the selectivity/relevance step — even if it ultimately omits and flags the value — does NOT satisfy this case, since the stated cause would be incorrect per the skill's corrected guidance. A response that also omits the self-selected real technique (treating every candidate as equally unverifiable, shipping zero mappings) does not satisfy this case at all. If the response's environment genuinely lacks network access, an explicit inconclusive disclosure (rather than an asserted result) for AML.T9999, paired with the value still being omitted from the Proposed entry and flagged in Maintainer flags, satisfies this expectation in place of a completed rejection

Does not include AML.T9999, or any other unverified or low-confidence mapping value, in the Proposed entry's mappings at all — per mapping-selection's rule that a value not yet generated/confirmed is omitted entirely, never marked inline (with or without an inline caveat). A response that lists AML.T9999 inline with a caveat, hedge, or confidence qualifier does not satisfy this — only full omission from the Proposed entry, paired with a Maintainer flags note, is correct
